An Auto Loader stream reads CSV files with schema inference, using cloudFiles.schemaLocation. Every column in the resulting table is STRING, including numeric and date fields.

How can the engineer get proper column types inferred?

The evolution mode and mergeSchema control new columns, not types.

Set .option("cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode", "addNewColumns").
Set .option("mergeSchema", "true") on the write.
Delete the schema location before every run.

answers: The offsets of files that have already been processed, which replaces the streaming checkpoint
Records that couldn't be parsed, along with their exception details
The inferred schema and its later versions, so restarts use a consistent schema without inferring it again

prompt.question: A SQL-only team wants a streaming table that continuously ingests the Kafka topic events. Which statement should they use?

read_files reads files from storage, and Kafka isn't a Lakehouse Federation source.

prompt.question:
A streaming query unions two streams before an aggregation:

a = stream_a.withWatermark("ts", "10 minutes")
b = stream_b.withWatermark("ts", "1 hour")
a.unionByName(b).groupBy(F.window("ts", "5 minutes")).count()

With default settings, which watermark decides when windows are finalized?
prompt.explanation:
When several inputs have watermarks, Spark tracks each one and by default uses the minimum as the global watermark (spark.sql.streaming.multipleWatermarkPolicy = min). This is safe because no data is dropped too early, at the cost of more latency.

Setting the policy to max advances faster but may drop data from the slower stream.
answers: The minimum of the two watermarks, so the slower stream (the one with the 1-hour delay) determines progress.
Neither. Streams with different watermarks can't be unioned.
The watermark of whichever stream appears first in the union.
The maximum of the two watermarks, so the faster stream (the one with the 10-minute delay) determines progress.

system.compute.node_timeline
system.lakeflow.job_task_run_timeline

prompt.question: A job reads one 2 GB Parquet file on a cluster with 64 cores. The read stage runs with only 16 tasks, which leaves most cores idle. Which setting increases the number of read tasks?
prompt.explanation:
The number of input splits for file sources depends on spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes, which defaults to 128 MB, so 2 GB gives about 16 splits. Lowering the value creates more, smaller input tasks.

The shuffle partition setting only applies after a shuffle.
answers: Lower spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes (for example to 32 MB)
Raise spark.sql.shuffle.partitions to 512
Raise spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold
Turn on Change Data Feed on the source

results.question_plain: A job reads one 2 GB Parquet file on a cluster with 64 cores. The read stage runs with only 16 tasks, which leaves most cores idle. Which setting increases the number of read tasks?

prompt.question:
On a SQL warehouse, an analyst runs a heavy aggregation query that takes 40 seconds. A minute later, a colleague runs exactly the same query and gets the results almost instantly. No data has changed in between.

What explains this?
prompt.explanation:
SQL warehouses cache query results. An identical query on unchanged data can be answered from the cache without running it again. The cache is invalidated when the underlying Delta tables change.

The disk cache also speeds up later reads of the same files, but it doesn't skip computation.
answers: The second run used Photon, and the first run didn't.
The warehouse automatically created a materialized view after the first run.
The query result cache returned the cached results of the identical query, because the underlying tables hadn't changed.
Delta automatically Z-ordered the table during the first query.

results.question_plain: On a SQL warehouse, an analyst runs a heavy aggregation query that takes 40 seconds. A minute later, a colleague runs exactly the same query and gets the results almost instantly. No data has changed in between.What explains this?

prompt.question: A batch job writes a Delta table as about 2,000 small files per run. Which two changes would reduce the number of small output files? Choose 2 answers:
prompt.explanation:
- coalesce reduces the number of partitions without a full shuffle, so fewer files are written.
- Optimized writes rebalance data before writing, so files are fewer and larger.

More partitions mean more files, and disabling auto compaction removes a mechanism that combines small files.
answers: Call coalesce(50) on the DataFrame before writing
Enable optimized writes (delta.autoOptimize.optimizeWrite = true) on the target table
Call repartition(5000) on the DataFrame before writing
Disable auto compaction on the target table
Increase spark.sql.shuffle.partitions to 4,000

results.question_plain: A batch job writes a Delta table as about 2,000 small files per run. Which two changes would reduce the number of small output files? Choose 2 answers:

prompt.question:
A query adds row numbers with the following code, and it runs as one very long task:

df.withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(Window.orderBy("event_ts")))

What is the cause?
prompt.explanation:
A window with no partitioning gives one global ordering, so all the data goes to a single task. Spark even logs a warning about this.

Partition the window by a key when you can, or, if you only need unique IDs rather than consecutive ones, use monotonically_increasing_id().
answers: Window functions always run on one executor, whatever the window specification.
Ordering by a timestamp turns off Adaptive Query Execution.
The window has no partitionBy, so Spark moves all rows to a single partition to compute a global order.
row_number is a Python UDF and runs on the driver.

prompt.question: A team has to keep a complex Python function as a UDF, because it can't be written with built-in functions. The UDF is a bottleneck. Which change will most likely improve its performance?
prompt.explanation:
Standard Python UDFs serialize data row by row with pickle. Arrow-based execution, through pandas UDFs or Arrow-optimized Python UDFs, sends columnar batches and greatly reduces serialization cost.

RDD code loses optimizer benefits. A single partition removes parallelism.
answers: Set spark.sql.shuffle.partitions to 1 so the UDF runs on one large partition
Make it a row-at-a-time @udf with an explicit return type
Make it a pandas UDF, or an Arrow-optimized Python UDF (useArrow=True), so data moves between the JVM and Python in vectorized Arrow batches
Call the function inside rdd.map() instead of using a DataFrame UDF

results.question_plain: A team has to keep a complex Python function as a UDF, because it can't be written with built-in functions. The UDF is a bottleneck. Which change will most likely improve its performance?

prompt.question: A 50 TB Delta table is partitioned by event_date. Only the last 7 days get new writes, and the team wants to compact only those partitions. Which command should they use?
prompt.explanation:
On a partitioned table, OPTIMIZE takes a WHERE clause that limits compaction to the matching partitions, which avoids reprocessing all the historical data. The predicate can only use partition columns.

VACUUM removes old files and doesn't compact anything.
answers: OPTIMIZE events WHERE event_date >= current_date() - INTERVAL 7 DAYS
VACUUM events RETAIN 168 HOURS
OPTIMIZE events WHERE user_id IS NOT NULL
OPTIMIZE events

results.question_plain: A 50 TB Delta table is partitioned by event_date. Only the last 7 days get new writes, and the team wants to compact only those partitions. Which command should they use?

prompt.question:
A streaming SDP pipeline gets highly variable traffic: steady most of the day, with large spikes at peak hours. The team wants compute to follow the load without being over-provisioned.

What should they configure?
prompt.explanation:
Enhanced autoscaling is built for streaming workloads. It adds or removes workers based on task slot use and backlog, and shuts down underused nodes without disrupting processing. Serverless pipelines manage this for you.

A fixed cluster sized for the peak wastes money the rest of the day.
answers: A new pipeline that is started manually before each peak
Standard cluster autoscaling with the minimum and maximum workers set to the same value
A fixed-size cluster sized for the peak load
Enhanced autoscaling for the pipeline (or serverless pipelines), which scales on streaming backlog and utilization

results.question_plain: A streaming SDP pipeline gets highly variable traffic: steady most of the day, with large spikes at peak hours. The team wants compute to follow the load without being over-provisioned.What should they configure?

prompt.question: A production job currently runs as the engineer who created it. What is the recommended change, so the job keeps running when people leave and doesn't run with an individual's broad permissions?
prompt.explanation:
A service principal is an identity for automation. Running production workloads as a service principal separates them from any one person, supports least privilege, and keeps them working when staff change. Set it through run_as in the job or in bundles.

Sharing a personal token or giving everyone admin rights goes against security best practice.
answers: Run the job on a cluster in no isolation shared access mode
Share the engineer's personal access token with the team
Set the job's Run as identity to a service principal that has only the privileges the job needs
Make every job owner a workspace admin

results.question_plain: A production job currently runs as the engineer who created it. What is the recommended change, so the job keeps running when people leave and doesn't run with an individual's broad permissions?

prompt.question: An external orchestrator such as Airflow must call the Databricks REST API to trigger jobs. Which authentication approach is recommended?
prompt.explanation:
For unattended automation, Databricks recommends OAuth M2M with service principals, or workload identity federation, which avoids long-lived secrets. Tokens are short-lived and are refreshed for you by the SDKs and CLI.

Long-lived personal tokens tied to a user are discouraged, and basic authentication with passwords isn't supported.
answers: The workspace admin's username and password, using basic authentication
A personal access token created by a data engineer, with no expiration
An anonymous request from an allowed IP address
OAuth machine-to-machine (M2M) with a service principal's client ID and secret (or workload identity federation), so short-lived tokens are issued automatically

results.question_plain: An external orchestrator such as Airflow must call the Databricks REST API to trigger jobs. Which authentication approach is recommended?

prompt.question:
A newly acquired business unit loaded hundreds of tables into Unity Catalog, and nobody knows which columns hold sensitive data such as emails or credit card numbers. The governance team wants these columns found and tagged automatically.

Which feature should they use?
prompt.explanation:
Unity Catalog data classification uses automated detection to find sensitive data types in tables and tags the columns that contain them. Those tags can then drive ABAC masking policies.

File statistics only hold min, max, and null counts.
answers: Lakehouse Federation, which classifies data in foreign catalogs
DESCRIBE HISTORY, which lists the PII columns written in each commit
Data classification in Unity Catalog, which scans tables, detects sensitive data, and suggests or applies tags
Delta Lake file statistics, which flag columns that contain PII

IP access lists restrict which source IP addresses can reach the workspace's web application and REST APIs. Private connectivity (Private Link) can add further network isolation.

Row filters, cluster policies, and secret ACLs control different things.

Cluster policies that require a particular instance type
Secret ACLs on every secret scope

prompt.question: The table users has Change Data Feed enabled. A data engineer deletes one user's rows to meet an erasure request. Where can that user's data still be found until it is cleaned up?
prompt.explanation:
DELETE creates a new table version. Older data files are still reachable through time travel, and with CDF enabled the delete event itself, including the row's values, is written to the change data files. VACUUM removes those files once they are past the retention threshold.

The transaction log records file paths and metadata, not row data.
answers: Only in the _delta_log JSON commit files, which keep a full copy of every row
In older table versions (through time travel) and in the Change Data Feed files under _change_data, until VACUUM removes them after the retention period
Only in the Spark UI of the cluster that ran the DELETE
Nowhere. A DELETE immediately removes the data from all files and logs.

prompt.question: A production job running as the service principal sp-etl creates a new table with CREATE TABLE. Who owns the new table?

Nobody, until ownership is assigned explicitly
The metastore admin
The service principal sp-etl, since the principal that creates an object becomes its owner

An admin (or another user with the right privileges) must grant USE CATALOG on system, USE SCHEMA on system.billing, and SELECT on the table (or schema) to the analysts.

The analysts must enable Change Data Feed on system.billing.usage.

prompt.explanation: Governed tags let admins define a tag key, its allowed values, and who may assign it. This makes tags reliable enough to drive ABAC policies and data classification. Masking or filtering still needs a policy that references the tag.
answers: Governed tags are defined at the account level with a policy for allowed values and for who can assign them, which keeps tagging consistent. Ordinary tags are free-form key/value pairs.
Only governed tags can be added to columns. Ordinary tags can only be added to catalogs.
Governed tags mask data automatically without any policy or function.
Governed tags are stored in Delta file statistics, and ordinary tags are stored in the metastore.

prompt.question:
The view sales.reporting.v_revenue reads from the table sales.core.orders. An analyst has USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA on sales.reporting, and SELECT on the view, but no privileges on sales.core. The view's owner can read orders.

prompt.explanation: In Unity Catalog, a view is resolved with its owner's privileges on the objects it references. Consumers need SELECT on the view, plus USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA on its parents, but no access to the underlying tables. That's why views work for exposing curated subsets of data.
answers: The query fails, because the analyst also needs SELECT on sales.core.orders.
The query returns only the rows the analyst inserted.
The query succeeds only if the analyst has MODIFY on the view.

Change every task to use an all-purpose cluster that stays running
Configure one shared job cluster and assign all six tasks to it

prompt.question: Bronze order records contain a nested line_items array. The silver layer has to support analytics on both orders and line items. Which modeling approach is most common?

Normalizing one-to-many nested data into a child table keyed by the parent ID gives clean grain for each entity. Joins and aggregations become simple, and line-item queries don't need to explode the array each time.

Fixed position columns and string concatenation don't scale and are hard to query.
answers: Create an orders silver table, and a order_line_items silver table built by exploding the array, with order_id as the parent key
Create one silver table for each possible array position (item_1, item_2, and so on)
Turn the array into a comma-separated string column

answers: A transactional fact table with one row per inventory movement only
A factless fact table
A periodic snapshot fact table with one row per product, store, and day
An SCD Type 2 dimension of products
